note.explanation: Within the elastic limit, a spring’s extension or compression is directly proportional to the force applied to it. The spring constant tells us how stiff the spring is.
examples: If a 10 N force stretches a spring by 0.02 m, k = F/x = 10/0.02 = 500 N m⁻¹.
For a spring with k = 200 N m⁻¹ stretched by 0.03 m, F = kx = 200 × 0.03 = 6 N.
note.simple: A stiffer spring needs more force for the same stretch.
note.checkQuestion: A spring with k = 300 N m⁻¹ is stretched by 0.02 m. What force is applied?
note.title: Hooke’s law and spring constant
steps: Substitute the force and extension, using extension in metres.
To find k, use k = F/x; to find F, use F = kx.
Give the unit of k as N m⁻¹.
note.answer: F = kx; the spring constant is k = F/x and is measured in N m⁻¹.

written.text: What is Hooke's law? Does an object remain elastic beyond elastic limit? Give reason.
written.finalAnswer: Within the elastic limit, the extension or compression of a spring is directly proportional to the applied force: F ∝ x or F = kx. An object does not remain elastic beyond its elastic limit because it becomes permanently deformed and no longer follows the linear force-extension relation.

written.text: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining: (i) the total extension in terms of x. (ii) the spring constant in terms of k. Arrangement: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom; two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.
written.finalAnswer: Series: total extension = 2x; spring constant = k/2. Parallel: total extension = x/2; spring constant = 2k.

rubric.why: Each series spring carries the load and extends by x.
rubric.description: Give the total extension for the series arrangement.
rubric.how: Add the two extensions, x + x = 2x.

rubric.why: The effective stiffness of two identical springs in series is lower.
rubric.description: Give the spring constant for the series arrangement.

rubric.why: In parallel, each identical spring shares half of the load and has the same extension.
rubric.description: Give the total extension for the parallel arrangement.
rubric.how: Each spring carries L/2, so its extension is half of x.

rubric.why: The combined stiffness of identical parallel springs adds.
rubric.description: Give the spring constant for the parallel arrangement.
rubric.how: Add the two spring constants: k + k = 2k.

modelAnswer: For one spring, L = kx.
Series: each spring carries L, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
k_series = L/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the two identical springs share the load equally, so each carries L/2.
Extension in parallel = (L/2)/k = x/2.
k_parallel = L/(x/2) = 2k.

written.text: Springs are made of steel instead of iron. Why?
written.finalAnswer: Steel is more elastic than iron: it returns to its original shape more readily when the deforming force is removed, provided its elastic limit is not exceeded.

explain.title: Hooke’s law
explain.body: If a force F is applied on a spring to stretch or compress it, the extension or compression x has been found directly proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit. Thus, F ∝ x or F = kx or k = F/x.

explain.title: Spring constant and stiffness
explain.body: where k is the constant of proportionality and is known as spring constant. In fact, it is a measure of stiffness of the spring. The greater the value of spring constant, the greater will be the stiffness or strength of the spring. Its unit is N m⁻¹.

explain.title: Force-extension graph
explain.body: A graph of force against extension is a straight line passing through the origin. The gradient or slope of force-extension graph is a measure of spring constant k. If the load exceeds the elastic limit, the spring is permanently deformed and the graph will no longer remain linear.

explain.title: Applications
explain.body: Springs are used in spring scales, the balance wheel of mechanical clocks and galvanometers. A spring scale measures weight from extension or compression; a clock spring controls back-and-forth motion; and a galvanometer’s hair spring helps restore its pointer to zero.

mistakes: Forgetting to state that Hooke’s law applies only within the elastic limit.
Using millimetres directly instead of converting extension to metres in a calculation for k in N m⁻¹.
Writing the spring constant unit as N instead of N m⁻¹.
Confusing the force-extension graph’s gradient with its intercept; its gradient represents k.
Saying a spring remains elastic beyond its elastic limit; beyond that limit it may be permanently deformed.
